habitat: Indochinese tigers inhabit the tropical and subtropical moist broadleaf forests, dry forests, and mountainous terrain of Southeast Asia, including Thailand, Myanmar, Laos, Vietnam, and Cambodia. Their habitat ranges from dense lowland rainforests to montane forests above 1,000 meters. The Mekong River basin forms much of their core range. Habitat loss from logging, agriculture, and hydroelectric dam construction has fragmented populations severely. They are now extinct in the wild in Vietnam, Cambodia, and possibly Laos.
diet: Indochinese tigers prey on wild boar, sambar and barking deer, gaur calves, serow, and occasionally porcupines and primates. They are solitary ambush hunters, relying on stealth, cover, and explosive speed over short distances rather than pursuit. A tiger may consume 15-40 kilograms of meat in a single feeding and can survive several days between kills. They are apex predators, and their presence indicates a healthy, intact ecosystem with sufficient prey populations.
behavior: Indochinese tigers are solitary and territorial, with males maintaining ranges of 100-300 square kilometers. They mark territory extensively through urine spraying, feces deposition, and tree scratching. They are primarily nocturnal and crepuscular, resting during the heat of the day in dense cover. Females give birth to 2-4 cubs after a gestation of 100-105 days. Cubs remain with their mother for 18-24 months, learning to hunt. They are powerful swimmers and readily cross rivers and lakes within their territory.
facts: The Indochinese tiger is darker and smaller than the Bengal tiger but larger than the Malayan and Sumatran subspecies. There are fewer than 350 remaining in the wild. In Thailand, the Huai Kha Khaeng Wildlife Sanctuary hosts the largest remaining population. DNA analysis confirmed this subspecies genetically in 2004. They are culturally significant across Southeast Asia, appearing in folklore, traditional medicine, and art. Tiger parts remain in demand on the black market, driving poaching despite international protection.
naming: Indochinese tiger names might reflect their Southeast Asian heritage or powerful presence. Consider names like Mekong, Rama (Thai king), Siam (historic name for Thailand), Khaeng (from Huai Kha Khaeng), Phaya (Thai for lord/ruler), Singh (lion in Sanskrit — also used for tigers), Jahangir (world-conqueror), or Indra (king of gods in Hindu mythology).
